items.text:
When Art told me what the topic of this conference was originally—NOTHING—I jumped at the chance to speak. That's easy... I can talk about nothing... I already have my talk prepared... Then he changed the topic... So I decided for this conference I would just ignore Art’s new topic and just go with the old “Nothing” topic.
Today, I am here to talk about NOTHING. Thank you.
Just kidding – I actually did that when I spoke at CCS graduation. When I walked off stage, I looked at the MC, who was in terror. What was she going to do? I could see it in her eyes as I walked by her. Then she started to go up to the stage to try to continue… I asked her later what she was going to say, and she said, "I don't know – probably 'thank you, Sir Norman, for that wonderful talk about nothing.' " As I thought about it, though, I actually think the concept of Nothing and a talk about Character, Calling, and Conviction really do have a lot in common. Let me explain.
All of us would have used one verse if we were doing a talk about nothing.

Apart from me you can do nothing. But what does that mean?
I think that when Jesus said “nothing,” he really meant nothing. Without Jesus, it is impossible for us to do anything. I don't think that those words of Jesus mean that we can’t do a lot, or that what we do will mean more if we do it with Him. I think what Jesus was saying was that whatever we do apart from Him IS nothing; it has no eternal value. NONE.
Now, it is important to understand what the context of this phrase was. What was He talking about when He said this?

He was talking about fruit. A vine and branches and fruit. Bearing fruit... abiding in Him... and if we abide... much fruit. I think we can agree from this verse that if we are not abiding in Him, we cannot produce fruit. None.
So, here is a question for you. Are Character, Calling and Conviction fruit? If you try hard enough by yourself, without Jesus, can you have good character? Can you strive to have a strong conviction? Can you be called to ANYTHING?
I think the best example I have of this is the disciples.
Let me ask a question. How did the disciples get their character, their calling and their conviction?
Did they get it when they walked with Jesus for three years? They heard every sermon. They saw every miracle. They had the best discipleship program in history, and the teacher was Jesus Himself. While He was here on earth they worked to understand. They tried to follow.
So, when Jesus was done teaching them, did they have it? What was the result of those three years? We don't have to guess.

After Jesus was gone they were huddled together in a locked room, afraid and shaking. They were destroyed. Jesus was dead. Their dreams were gone. Their conviction was lost. Their character? Quitters! Their calling? A lost dream. The one they believed in was dead. Now what? They said "Let's hide and hopefully they don’t find us and kill us."
After all the time with Jesus. After all the miracles. After all His teaching. After the countless discussions over dinner. After all the personal one-on-one time. ALL of them left . ALL of them left their conviction in the dust. They were failures and losers. Now what? All of their plans, their calling to change the world... all gone.
It is obvious that even after being with Jesus… even after all their effort and trying… NONE of them developed true character, NONE of them developed conviction to die for what they believed, NONE of them knew what it really meant to be called.
In Mark, they all deserted Him and fled.
In Luke, Peter denied Jesus three times.
In John, after the cross, where do we find them? Behind locked doors and afraid. The men who would one day turn the world upside down were hiding in a room. No real convictions, no real character and no real calling.
And that would have been the end. ... As Jesus had already predicted it… their character, their calling and their conviction were NOTHING without Him. In fact, they weren't theirs at all.

Then Jesus was back, he spent more time with them. When he was leaving... Acts 1:6 – Then they gathered around him and asked him, “Lord, are you at this time going to restore the kingdom to Israel?”
Can you picture the scene as the disciples, excited to see Jesus back from the dead, ask this question in Acts 1:6: "Lord, are you at this time going to restore the kingdom to Israel?"
I am sure they thought, "Finally… now we can get going again. Jesus is back and nothing is going to stop us now!"
They still didn't get it. Is now the time? You're going to restore your kingdom and it is easy for us! They were looking for the easy way out. Now I really don't need conviction or character or calling. You set up your kingdom and we are in charge now. The hard part is over.
But no, the hard part wasn't over—but something WAS going to change.

Acts 1:8 - But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you;
That next phrase brought even more excitement. I am sure they thought, "Awesome! We get power!" but little did they know what lay ahead. Although it was full of power, it was also full of trials, hard times, persecutions and even death.
If I want to experience the power of God in my life, I should expect nothing different. It is His power, but in the midst of difficulties, hard times and struggles.
"You shall receive power" will bring opposition.
"You shall receive power" will bring difficulties.
"You shall receive power" will bring hard times. It will bring jail.
"You shall receive power" will bring conflict. It will bring thorns in the flesh.
"You shall receive power" WILL reveal our weakness.
But then...
In our weakness He is strong.
In our weakness He works in mighty ways.
In our weakness He brings healing.
In our weakness He saves people. He brings revival, He transforms us.
In our weakness He changes the world.
Don't expect that "you shall receive power" will look any different in your life than it did for the disciples.

And look at what happened next. Within a few chapters, Peter and John are in jail. Then all the apostles are arrested, flogged, and ordered never to speak in the name of Jesus again.
Stephen is stoned. James is killed with the sword. The church is scattered. They expected a throne; they got a difficult road.
When Jesus calls Paul, He tells Ananias, "This man is my chosen instrument," and in the same breath, "I will show him how much he must suffer for my name." The calling and the suffering came in the same sentence.
The word Jesus used for witness is martys, the word we get martyr from. When He said, "You will be my witnesses," they had no idea yet what that word would come to mean.
The disciples received power, and it brought prison, conflict, and weakness.
So don't expect it to look any different for you. I think a lot of us in ministry carry a quiet expectation: If I'm really called, if God's power is really on me, things should go well. The church should grow. The money should come in. The board should agree with me. And when it doesn't, we wonder what we did wrong.
Maybe we didn't do anything wrong. Maybe that's just what the power looks like.

But look at what happened to these men. The same Peter who couldn't stand up to a servant girl by a fire now stands up before the Sanhedrin, the most powerful men in Jerusalem.
And the leaders looked at Peter and John, saw that they were unschooled, ordinary men, and they were astonished. And they took note that these men had been with Jesus.
Where did that courage come from? Where did that character come from? Not from a seminar. Not from trying harder.
Character, calling, conviction. They didn't make themselves. His power produced them.

Now, we can argue a lot about what that power is supposed to look like and what it is supposed to do. Some of us say the power is about miracles and healing and signs. Some of us say God doesn't really work that way anymore. And we could spend this whole conference debating it.
I don't want to debate that today. I want to suggest that maybe we're asking the wrong question. We keep asking what the power does. I believe Jesus was describing what the power would produce in them. He didn't say, "You will do witnessing." He said, "You will be my witnesses."
His power isn't about how we change ourselves. It's about what He makes us into.

The word Jesus uses for power in Acts 1:8 is *dynamis*. And it is the same word Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 12:9, when the Lord tells him, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness."
Same word. Same power.
We get our word "dynamite" from it, and we love that. We want the dynamite. But look where Paul found it. He had begged God three times to take his thorn away, and God said no. So Paul says, "I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ's power may rest on me... For when I am weak, then I am strong."

Go back to Peter. Peter was the strong one. He was the first to speak, the first to step out of the boat, the first to pull out a sword in the garden. He cut off a man's ear. That was strength without character.
Peter was the one who said, "Even if all fall away, I will not." That was his conviction, and he meant it. But it was his conviction, not God's. And it failed him by a fire, in front of a servant girl. Luke tells us that the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter, and Peter went outside and wept bitterly. That night by the fire, something in Peter broke. And it had to.
Before God could use Peter, he had to break Peter's self-sufficiency. I believe God cannot use someone who is not broken—someone who has stopped relying on their own strength and started relying on the strength of the One living in them—Christ.

Watchman Nee said, "Effort is not the key to maturity; death is." That is not the kind of thing you put on a leadership poster.
We spend our whole lives striving to be strong when God is calling us to be weak.

My dad, Gene Denler, was a missionary here in the Philippines for about thirty years with the Navigators. He was very effort‑focused. It was always, "It's you, it's you."
He left the field feeling broken. He wondered what his life had really accomplished, and he ended up working as a construction supervisor for my uncle. As he got older, he came to see that it was never about his effort; it was about Christ. By the time he died, he was a different person.
In 2009, when he was 81, my dad came back to the Philippines. He ended up in the hospital with blood clots in both legs, at St. Luke's, the same hospital where I was born. And because of that interruption, he got to sit with some of the men he had discipled as teenagers forty years earlier, still serving God in their sixties. He wrote in his journal, "It humbled me to realize anew that we sow, we water, but it's God who makes it grow."
On that same trip, he wrote about what he called "a faulty ministry model" that had been part of his DNA—the idea that you have to aggressively make it happen through strategies and programs. And he wrote about being drawn instead to the way Jesus simply went about doing good and building relationships. He ended it with three words: "He is enough!"

So let me ask you. ... Are you broken?
Someone once said, "In the ministry of love, only the wounded can serve." I would add to that: one of the requirements of serving is being wounded, being broken. I think we all need to ask the question... Am I broken? And when we say yes, and we really feel that way inside—that is when He uses us in mighty ways. Until then it is just us and our effort... another word for that is NOTHING.
Maybe you came to this conference broken. Maybe it’s your church, your marriage, your finances, or your own heart. Maybe, like my dad, you feel like your work has come to nothing. Let me say this: you are QUALIFIED!
Maybe you came and feel good about all you do, and how much you are doing for God. Deep down inside you kind of feel like, "God is really lucky to have me!" The word "NOTHING" comes back to my mind. God cannot use someone who is not broken.
If you are broken, you're exactly where He wants you to be. That isn’t the end of your ministry. It may be the beginning of it.

In Japan there's an art called kintsugi. When a bowl breaks, they don't throw it away. They put it back together with gold. And the bowl becomes more valuable than it was before it broke. The cracks are where the gold is.
Paul says, "We have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this all-surpassing power is from God and not from us."

Paul says suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance produces character. Character isn't something you build on a good day.
Character, calling, conviction. We don't make them. His power makes them in our weakness.
In 2017, when I came to the ministry, I had a lot to learn about not relying on my own strength. I recently made a short video talking about this.

Another story. One day in 2020, Art and I were sitting around a table, talking about the feeding program. We had run out of money. The feedings needed to stop. Pastor Art looked at me and said, "We can't stop. There are people who are hungry, Norman." I told him I didn't know what to do, but we HAD to stop.
I remember it as if it was yesterday: I got up and walked away from the table, looked at my phone, and there was an email from my former boss. He is not even a Christian. He was letting me know that the board of their foundation was sending $50,000 to help with the feeding program.
I walked back to the table and told Art, "Never mind. The money came in. God provided."
I didn't raise that money. I walked away from that table with nothing, and God was already there. And we have so many stories from that season during COVID, just like that one.

I used to windsurf. When you windsurf, you don't make the wind. You can't. You can pull on that sail as hard as you want, and if there's no wind, you go nowhere. But when the wind comes and you catch it, you fly. You're still working. Every muscle is working. But it doesn't drain you. It's the most fun you'll ever have.
That's what Paul means in Colossians 1:29: "To this end I strenuously contend with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in me." Paul is working hard, but the energy is Christ's.
When I strive in my strength, I burn out. When I strive in His, I'm refreshed.
So that's what I learned. I'm not the strong one; I never was. It's the same pattern we saw in Peter and in my dad. God let the strength run out so He could be the strength.

Character, calling, and conviction sound very tidy, don't they? Like something you could put in a box and check off. Character, check. Calling, check. Conviction, check. Sounds like someone with OCD - everything in order. Shirts organized by color in their closet.
The opposite is true. They are more like a painter's palette.
Look at a painter's palette. It's a mess. Colors smeared everywhere, blobs, drips, brushes dipped in three colors at once. If all you ever saw was the palette, you'd say, what a mess. But somewhere behind it, there's a painting. Every beautiful painting started on a messy palette.
Ministry is messy, and there's beauty in the mess. If life were all straight lines, we wouldn't need God. And I've come to believe God intentionally puts us right where the mess shows up, so that He can be the one who makes it work.
The mess teaches us humility. I'm not in control, and I can't fix it.
And if I expect it to be clean, I will be disappointed, and then I will be angry—angry at my staff, angry at the board, angry at the pastors who didn't show up, and, if I'm honest, angry at God.
Even right now, at KIDS, it is a messy ministry. Relationship issues, money issues, kids in the home and school making bad decisions, water bills are high due to a leak, challenges on the boards, people not getting along.
It's messy.
And I am seeing God at work everywhere in the middle of it.
So expect the mess. And expect God in it.

Now, that doesn't mean we go looking for a mess, or that we create one. Some of us are very good at creating it. We bring God's order into it.
That's what Christ did. He didn't stand outside our mess and tell us to clean it up. He came right down into the middle of it. "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us."
He was born in a barn and laid in a feeding trough with the animals. That is about as messy as it gets. God's answer to our mess wasn't a memo. It was a baby in a manger.

And when you're in the middle of the mess, remember this.
My dad used to tell me a story about him and his brother going to the circus. They would watch through a knothole in the fence, and they saw one animal at a time going by. Then they decided to climb up a tree, and from there they saw the whole circus at one glance. My dad then said, "God sees every episode of our lives at one glance."
So don't judge your ministry by one frame. And don't judge anyone else's by one frame, either. He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion.
God doesn't just see a point in time. He sees the whole journey.

Remember, Paul wrote some of his most beautiful letters from prison. Right in the middle of the mess, God was using him. He wrote Philippians—a letter about joy—in chains. The mess didn't stop what God was doing. The mess was where God was doing it on purpose. And in that same letter, he writes, "It is God who works in you to will and to act in order to fulfill His good purpose"—from a prison cell. He was in prison to fulfill God's good purpose.
Character, calling, conviction. We don't make them. They are made in the mess.

The mess is where the power lives.
Think about the manger—the animals, the poop, the smell. And that's where the power came from.
Think about the cross. From the outside, it looked like the biggest mess in all of history: the Son of God, beaten, mocked, hanging between two criminals, His friends gone. Yet it was the greatest display of God's power the world has ever seen.
Paul says, "The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. The weakness of God is stronger than human strength."

The disciples asked for a kingdom, and Jesus gave them power. But it didn't make life easier; it made them different. Peter had his own conviction: "I will never deny you." And it failed him by a fire, in front of a servant girl. Then, through prison, persecution, and failure, God did what Peter never could: He formed a character that was God's caracter, made clear a calling that was God's calling, and planted a conviction that was God's convistion. It still works that way today.
Today we are doing a set of sessions on these three important topics: Character, Calling, and Conviction.
I pray that God Himself will create His character, calling and conviction in you.
